# Spoked wheels, pivoting axles and sprung carriages (`spoked_wheel_suspension_carriage`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by bloomery_iron, horse_collar_harness, ball_bearings
- Core idea: A light spoked wheel with a hot-shrunk iron tyre is strong yet light; dish the wheel (spokes slightly conical) so it resists sideways shocks. Pivot the front axle on a kingpin so the wagon can turn, and hang the body on leather straps or, better, steel leaf springs so road shocks do not reach the passengers or break the load. Grease the axles; friction and bad roads, not the horse, are usually the limit.
- Pitfalls:
  - Suggesting wheeled vehicles to the Americas as a missing idea; wheels were known on toys, but the Inca had extensive roads for people and pack llamas, and wheeled haulage had different terrain and traction requirements
  - Thinking a rigid wagon body on bare axles is acceptable for passengers or glass
  - Assuming all spoked wheels need dishing or iron tyres; early chariot wheels used other constructions
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3500–3200 BC – solid wheels (also Central Europe, Ljubljana wheel c. 3150 BC); global: c. 2000 BC – spoked chariot wheels in the Sintashta culture (southern Urals steppe); egypt: c. 1600 BC – chariots arrive with the Hyksos; china: c. 1200 BC – chariots at Anyang; americas: 1st millennium AD – wheeled figurines in Mesoamerica (Veracruz), no wheeled transport; europe: 1st millennium BC – archaeological evidence for pivoting front axles on European wagons; 15th c. – coach (kocsi) associated with Kocs, Hungary; 1804 Elliott's elliptic springs
- Read:
  - David W. Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007)
  - M. G. Lay, Ways of the World: A History of the World's Roads and of the Vehicles That Used Them (1992)
